title: Building an Algo-Trading Platform: 56K Lines of Code, but My Biggest Challenge Isn't the Strategy
author: BlackGreep
selftext:
\*\*Title: Building an algo-trading research platform — 56k lines of code, and our biggest challenge isn't the strategy\*\*

I'm building BlackGreep, a trading research and strategy-validation platform.

The idea is simple: \*\*validate a strategy before risking real money.\*\*

Here's where the project currently stands:

\* 56,658 lines of code, including 25,616 lines of tests.
\* 287 code files.
\* Latest focused regression run: 572 passed, 1 skipped.
\* Backtesting, data integrity, risk controls, and research infrastructure under development.

But none of those numbers proves we have a profitable trading strategy.

\*\*Our latest architecture review exposed a more interesting problem.\*\*

We've implemented several security components independently:

1. Cryptographically signed data-access approvals.
2. Durable approval reservations using SQLite.
3. Signed checkpoints designed to detect ledger rollback.
4. Windows file-identity checks and bounded acquisition.
5. Separate migration and research-worker permission contracts.

The problem?

These components aren't yet connected through a single enforced execution flow.

We need to guarantee the correct order:

\*\*Verify approval → reserve access → acknowledge checkpoint → allow data acquisition.\*\*

If any stage fails, the file must not be opened.

We're implementing a synthetic integration test to verify that behavior, including crash recovery, replay attempts, and concurrent operations.

The other challenge is preventing out-of-sample contamination.

Our planned dataset uses separate Discovery, Validation, and protected Holdout periods. Some historical source files cross the Validation/Holdout boundary, so even preparing the research dataset requires careful isolation.

We're evaluating a separate offline migration environment so the research process receives only approved pre-Holdout data.

\*\*Important:\*\* Our current tests are predominantly synthetic. Production Windows isolation is not proven, real source migration hasn't happened, and independent Validation is still pending.

I'd rather discover a broken assumption now than publish misleading performance numbers later.

\*\*Question for people building serious trading research systems:\*\*

Would you favor a disposable offline migration VM or dedicated Windows worker accounts with strict filesystem permissions to prevent accidental Holdout access?

And what additional failure modes would you test before trusting the setup?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: For a one-time job like splitting the mixed files, I'd pick the disposable offline VM: it starts clean, the research side never shares a disk with it, and when the migration is done you delete it, which leaves no leftover permissions to get wrong. Dedicated Windows accounts are fine for the day-to-day research worker, but file permissions are easy to misconfigure and hard to prove, so I'd keep the research side on a machine that only ever receives the canonical partitions. Failure modes I'd test: a crash between the checkpoint and the file open, the same approval replayed after a restart, clock changes that make an approval look newer or expired, and a backup or sync tool (like OneDrive or antivirus) that reads the protected files on its own. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to see how strategy results get compared against a benchmark.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's a useful recommendation. I'm leaning toward a disposable offline migration VM as well, with the research environment receiving only independently verified canonical partitions.

The failure modes you listed are especially relevant. We're currently preparing a synthetic integration test for the reservation → checkpoint acknowledgement → file-open sequence, including crashes and replay after restart.

The backup/sync/antivirus angle is a good addition. We also need to verify shared folders, mounted volumes, VM snapshots, and background processes before claiming isolation.

Actual OS isolation hasn't been proven yet, so we're keeping real-data migration blocked until those boundaries are tested.

Thanks for the detailed feedback.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good call keeping the real-data migration blocked until the boundaries are tested. One more thing to add to the shared-folder and snapshot check: clipboard and drag-and-drop between host and VM, since those are easy to forget and can move a file across without anyone noticing. Thanks for the clear exchange.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Good catch. Clipboard sharing and drag-and-drop are easy-to-miss transfer paths.

We'll include them explicitly in the offline VM isolation checklist, alongside shared folders, mounted drives, snapshots, and background sync processes.

The intended handoff is a controlled export of verified pre-Holdout canonical data, not general file sharing between environments.

Thanks for pointing that out.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good plan, and testing denial with real restricted identities, including spawned subprocesses and symlinks, is the right way to prove it. One more path worth adding to the list is the host itself: if the host runs backup or sync software, a VM snapshot or the VM disk file can be copied out with the protected data inside it, so keep the VM’s disk image out of any synced folder.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's an important distinction. An offline VM doesn't guarantee offline data handling if the host can back up or sync the VM disk itself.

We'll include host-level backup and sync processes in the isolation threat model, and keep VM disk images and snapshots outside automatically synchronized locations.

This will also need to be verified before real-data migration, rather than assumed from the VM configuration.

Appreciate the detailed feedback.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Sounds good. A cheap way to verify the host side is to search the backup or sync tool's own file list and logs after a test run, looking for any file name or hash from the protected set. If it never appears there, that's evidence the VM disk and snapshots are out of its reach. Thanks for the open discussion.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's exactly the distinction we're aiming for: OS-enforced isolation, including subprocesses, not just application-level checks.

Right now, our role and filesystem contracts have only been tested in synthetic scenarios. We haven't proven actual OS-level denial yet, and I'm not treating those tests as proof of production security.

The direction we're evaluating is a disposable offline migration VM that handles the original sources, followed by a controlled export of verified, immutable pre-Holdout canonical partitions to a separate research environment.

Before allowing real-data migration, I want to test actual access denial under restricted research-worker identities, including spawned subprocesses, symlinks, reparse points, and alternate filesystem paths.

The research environment should never receive the original mixed files or protected Holdout sources.

Of course, that still depends on the host and virtualization boundaries being trustworthy.

Interesting to hear you're building TIYlab. How are you approaching process isolation and verification in your own system?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Small correction: I’m not building TIYlab, that name seems to have been mixed up, so I can’t speak to its isolation approach. What I can add is a habit from testing this kind of boundary: make the denial test part of the pipeline so it runs every time, with a file that must fail to open, and treat a pass as a stop condition.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
You're right, I mixed up the TIYlab reference with another commenter. Sorry about that.

The denial-test suggestion is excellent. I agree it should be a mandatory pre-migration gate, not just an occasional security test.

We'll need both positive access controls and negative tests under actual restricted worker identities, including subprocesses.

If a protected test file can be opened, the entire operation must stop.

Thanks for the clarification and the practical suggestion.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: No problem, easy mix-up with a long thread. One small addition: run the denial test from the same account and the same kind of process the research worker will use, and also after any permission change or restart, since that's when a rule quietly stops applying. Thanks for the clear exchange.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Agreed. Testing under the actual research worker identity and process context is essential.

We'll include mandatory access-denial checks after restarts and permission changes, not just during initial deployment.

If a protected test file becomes accessible, the workflow must fail closed before any real-data operation.

Thanks again for the practical advice!

comments.author: Luger99
comments.body: Dumb question.  How do you handle splits and corporate actions?  These have been one of the more problematic/computationally intensive part of my work as they impact the history as the data set walks forward.  Ultimately what i have built will work, but the processing time has gotten long.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Not a dumb question at all.

Our current dataset focuses on BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, and SOLUSDT on Bybit Linear, so traditional stock splits and corporate actions aren't part of the current pipeline.

We haven't implemented an equities corporate-action adjustment engine yet.

If we expand into equities, I'd prefer a versioned corporate-action event ledger with point-in-time adjustments and incremental recomputation of affected partitions, rather than rebuilding the entire dataset after every change.

Out of curiosity, is your main bottleneck recalculating adjusted historical prices or replaying the entire dataset?

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
The distinction between passing component tests and proving an enforced boundary is the important one here.

I'd lean toward a disposable offline migration VM, but I'd make the handoff strictly one-way.

The migration process would produce immutable pre-holdout datasets alongside a manifest containing file hashes, source versions and permitted date ranges.

The research workers would only receive those approved outputs, never access to the original mixed files.

For the "no file open on failure" requirement, I'd test the boundary at the OS level, not just through application logs.

That includes attempts through symbolic links, Windows reparse points, file replacement between approval and opening, and crashes at every stage of the authorization sequence.

I'm building TIYlab, a non-custodial Bitcoin portfolio automation project. It's a different system, but I share your view that passing isolated tests isn't the same as proving end-to-end safety.

One question: are you planning to verify that the research worker and its subprocesses cannot access the holdout at all, or only that your application code refuses to open it?

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: Disposable VM all day. Permissions are easy to misconfigure and impossible to prove, and one accidental holdout read torches your whole validation. Delete the VM and there's nothing left to leak.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
I'm leaning toward a disposable offline VM as well, especially since this is a one-time migration rather than a permanent data-processing service.

I agree that a single unintended Holdout exposure can compromise the independence of the evaluation.

The important caveat is that deleting the VM doesn't undo data already copied through shared folders, snapshots, clipboard, or background processes.

So the plan is to verify isolation first, then allow only a controlled export of validated pre-Holdout partitions.

Thanks for the input.
